rawInput.complaint:
A 45-year-old man was referred for evaluation of proteinuria. He had noted occult blood in his urine since age 24. At age 37, hypertension was diagnosed, and laboratory tests showed microscopic hematuria and proteinuria of 0.4 g/g creatinine. Over the next eight years, proteinuria gradually increased to 1.16 g/g creatinine, prompting hospital admission.

He denied episodes of gross hematuria or flank pain. He was born at term; birth weight was unknown. There was no family history of kidney disease. Medications included losartan (25 mg daily), amlodipine (5 mg daily), and febuxostat (20 mg daily). He weighed 98.7 kg and was 177 cm tall (BMI 31.5 kg/m^2) and had been overweight (BMI >25) since adolescence. Blood pressure was 140/78 mm Hg.

Physical examination was unremarkable. Urinalysis showed proteinuria of 0.7 g/g creatinine, 10–19 red blood cells per high-power field, and red-cell casts. Serum creatinine was 0.69 mg/dL, cystatin C 0.74 mg/L, albumin 4.1 g/dL, uric acid 6.3 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 144 mg/dL, and HbA1c 5.5%. Estimated GFR was 97.6 mL/min/1.73 m^2. C-reactive protein, IgG, IgA, complement levels, and ANA were within normal limits. ECG and chest radiograph were normal. Renal ultrasonography showed bilaterally normal-sized kidneys with preserved cortical thickness.

With a clinical suspicion of IgA nephropathy, a kidney biopsy was performed.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief concern is chronic urinary abnormalities progressing over many years: occult blood in the urine since age 24, later development of hypertension at age 37, and gradually increasing proteinuria from 0.4 g/g creatinine to 1.16 g/g creatinine over 8 years. At admission he still had preserved kidney function but persistent glomerular urinary findings.

Salient positive findings point to a chronic glomerular process. Urinalysis showed proteinuria (0.7 g/g creatinine), microscopic hematuria (10–19 RBCs/HPF), and importantly red-cell casts, which strongly localize bleeding to the glomerulus. Hypertension is present (140/78 mm Hg on losartan and amlodipine). The course is indolent over decades, beginning in young adulthood. Renal function is preserved: creatinine 0.69 mg/dL, cystatin C 0.74 mg/L, eGFR 97.6 mL/min/1.73 m^2, albumin 4.1 g/dL, and kidneys are normal-sized on ultrasound. He is obese (BMI 31.5) and has been overweight since adolescence, which raises the possibility of obesity-related glomerulopathy, but that alone would not explain the persistent microscopic hematuria with red-cell casts.

Pertinent negatives help narrow the differential. He denied gross hematuria and flank pain, arguing against nephrolithiasis or episodic urologic bleeding. Normal CRP, ANA, complements, and immunoglobulins make systemic inflammatory or immune-complex diseases such as lupus nephritis or infection-related GN less likely. There is no family history of kidney disease, which makes hereditary nephritis such as Alport syndrome or thin basement membrane disease less likely, though not impossible. Normal serum albumin and only subnephrotic proteinuria argue against nephrotic syndromes such as primary FSGS or membranous nephropathy as the main presentation. Normal ultrasound with preserved cortical thickness argues against advanced chronic structural kidney disease.

The leading differential is IgA nephropathy because it commonly presents with persistent microscopic hematuria, variable proteinuria, hypertension, and preserved renal function for years. Red-cell casts support glomerulonephritis, and the long indolent course from young adulthood fits well. Although serum IgA is normal and there is no history of gross hematuria, neither finding excludes IgA nephropathy.

A second consideration is obesity-related glomerulopathy/FSGS, supported by longstanding obesity, hypertension, and proteinuria. However, this diagnosis is less convincing because obesity-related glomerulopathy typically causes proteinuria with bland urine sediment, whereas this patient has longstanding microscopic hematuria and red-cell casts, which are much more suggestive of a primary glomerulonephritis.

Another consideration is thin basement membrane nephropathy or Alport-spectrum disease because of isolated hematuria beginning at a young age. But progressive proteinuria, hypertension, and red-cell casts favor a more inflammatory glomerular disease, and there is no family history or extrarenal features provided.

Other immune-complex or systemic glomerulonephritides are less likely given normal complements, negative ANA, lack of systemic symptoms, and the very chronic stable course.

Overall, the combination of decades-long microscopic hematuria, subnephrotic but increasing proteinuria, hypertension, red-cell casts, preserved renal function, and absence of systemic disease most strongly supports IgA nephropathy as the single most likely diagnosis.

differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Chronic microscopic hematuria since age 24, increasing subnephrotic proteinuria, hypertension, and red-cell casts indicating glomerular bleeding; long indolent course with preserved renal function is typical.
BMI 31.5 with longstanding overweight, hypertension, and proteinuria could fit; however persistent hematuria and red-cell casts are less typical and argue against it as the primary diagnosis.
